meta.name: Greyhound Grooming Guide
meta.excerpt: The Greyhound is probably the easiest large breed to groom. The coat takes five minutes a week. The teeth, however, are a different story — dental disease is the #1 health issue in the breed and daily brushing is non-negotiable.

intro.label: Overview
intro.heading: The Easiest Large-Breed Coat — And the One Grooming Task That's Not Easy
intro.html:
The Greyhound coat is genuinely minimal maintenance. Short, smooth, single-layered, and naturally low-odor — a weekly pass with a soft brush takes five minutes and that's essentially the full coat care routine. There's no undercoat to manage, no feathering to tangle, no seasonal coat blows. If the coat were the whole story, this would be the shortest grooming guide on the site.

But there are two things about Greyhounds that require real, consistent attention: their teeth and their skin. Dental disease is the #1 health issue in the breed — they have thin tooth enamel, crowded dentition, and develop tartar unusually fast. Without daily brushing, most Greyhounds need professional dental cleanings every 12–18 months, often with extractions. This isn't optional maintenance; it's the difference between a healthy mouth and a painful, expensive problem.

The skin concern is structural: with almost no body fat, Greyhounds develop pressure sores quickly on hard surfaces. This is a bedding issue more than a grooming one, but it's worth understanding: check elbows and hips regularly for any thickening or rawness.

care.label: Tools & Routine
care.heading: The Routine That Actually Matters
care.html:
Tools You Need

  • Soft bristle brush or grooming mitt — the only brush you need for a Greyhound coat; a rubber grooming glove also works well and most dogs enjoy the sensation
  • Dog toothbrush and enzymatic toothpaste — the most important grooming tool you own for this breed; use daily
  • Dog winter coat (1–2) — not optional in cold climates; Greyhounds have no insulating undercoat and minimal body fat; they get cold quickly and genuinely need a coat below about 45°F

Grooming Routine

FrequencyTask
DailyTeeth brushing — enzymatic toothpaste; 2 minutes; non-negotiable for this breed
Once a weekSoft brush or grooming mitt — full body; 5–10 minutes; removes dust and loose hairs
WeeklyCheck elbows and hip points for pressure sores — any thickening or redness indicates inadequate bedding
Every 6–8 weeksBath — Greyhounds are naturally low-odor; no need to bathe more frequently; use a gentle dog shampoo and dry thoroughly
Every 3–4 weeksNail trim — nails grow fast in athletic breeds; long nails affect gait and posture
Every 12–18 monthsProfessional dental cleaning under anesthesia — standard of care for this breed; more frequently if brushing is inconsistent

How to Start Teeth Brushing

The biggest obstacle to daily teeth brushing is a dog that won't tolerate it. Build the habit incrementally:

  • Week 1: Let them lick the enzymatic toothpaste off your finger, nothing more
  • Week 2: Run your finger along the gum line with toothpaste applied
  • Week 3: Introduce the toothbrush briefly — a few teeth, then stop
  • Week 4 onward: Full brushing session, building to 2 full minutes

Always use dog toothpaste — human toothpaste contains fluoride and xylitol, both of which are toxic to dogs. Enzymatic formulas work even if you don't get perfect technique; the enzymes continue breaking down bacteria after you stop brushing.

special.label: Breed-Specific Tips
special.heading: Greyhound-Specific Grooming Considerations
special.html:
Cold Weather and the Winter Coat

Greyhounds don't have the fat reserves or the undercoat that other breeds use to regulate temperature. In temperatures below 45°F (7°C), most Greyhounds need a coat for outdoor walks — not as a comfort choice, but as a temperature regulation necessity. In hard winters below freezing, a lined coat is required, not optional. Many owners keep a rain jacket for wet weather and an insulated coat for cold; the dog will make it very clear if they're cold by shivering, reluctance to go outside, and tucking their tail.

Anesthesia and Dental Cleanings

Professional dental cleanings require anesthesia — and Greyhound anesthesia sensitivity is a critical medical fact every owner needs to know. Greyhounds metabolize barbiturate-based anesthetics differently due to their low body fat and different liver enzyme profile. Any veterinarian performing a dental cleaning on a Greyhound must use propofol-based or isoflurane protocols, not older barbiturate-based ones. Before any dental cleaning, confirm your vet has experience with sighthounds. The adoption organization you got your Greyhound from can usually recommend a sighthound-aware practice.

Pressure Sore Prevention

Greyhounds sleep 16–18 hours a day with almost no body fat between their bony prominences and whatever surface they're lying on. A thick orthopedic or memory foam dog bed isn't a luxury — it prevents calluses and open pressure sores that become infected and require vet treatment. Check elbows and hip points weekly. Any thickening, dark discoloration, or raw patches indicate inadequate bedding or too much time on hard floors. Many Greyhound owners simply give them couch access as the practical solution.

faq.a: Not for their coat — the short, single-layer coat requires no trimming and minimal brushing. The professional intervention that matters for Greyhounds is dental cleaning under anesthesia, typically needed every 12–18 months. That's a veterinary procedure, not a grooming appointment. Beyond that, nail trims (which can be done at a groomer or vet) are the other recurring professional need.

faq.q: How bad is Greyhound dental disease really?
faq.a: Serious enough that it's consistently cited as the breed's #1 health issue. Greyhounds have thin tooth enamel, teeth that are positioned more closely together than most breeds, and a tendency to develop heavy tartar unusually fast. Without daily brushing, tooth loss and periodontal disease requiring extractions are common by middle age. Daily brushing + annual dental check + professional cleaning every 1–2 years is the standard of care, not an optional extra.

faq.q: My Greyhound won't let me brush their teeth. What do I do?
faq.a: Build tolerance gradually over 3–4 weeks rather than forcing the issue. Start with just letting them lick enzymatic toothpaste off your finger — no brush at all. Progress to running a toothpaste-coated finger along the gum line. Introduce the brush only once the finger touch is comfortable. Enzymatic toothpaste does some work even without perfect technique, but actual brushing action is meaningfully more effective. Daily consistency matters more than duration.

faq.q: Does a Greyhound really need a dog coat?
faq.a: Yes, in cold weather. This isn't anthropomorphism — it's anatomy. With almost no body fat and a single short coat, Greyhounds lose core body heat quickly in cold temperatures. Most Greyhounds start shivering visibly below 45°F. A properly fitted dog coat for winter walks is a genuine comfort and health need. Measure around the neck, chest, and from neck to base of tail to find a good fit — Greyhound proportions (deep chest, narrow waist) can make standard coats fit poorly.

faq.q: How do I prevent pressure sores on a Greyhound?
faq.a: Provide adequate cushioned sleeping surfaces everywhere the dog rests. An orthopedic or memory foam bed at least 3 inches thick is the baseline. If they're on hard floors for significant parts of the day, that will eventually cause callusing and open sores on elbows and hips. Check these points weekly. Early-stage calluses can be managed with regular application of a dog-safe balm (paw butter works well); open sores need vet attention.
